headings.title: Anatomy and Protective Structures of the Eye
headings.content:
The eye sits securely within the bony orbit of the skull, a protective socket that cushions the globe against physical trauma. Several accessory structures cooperate to shield and maintain the delicate surface of the eye. 

- **Eyelids (Palpebrae)**: Mechanical barriers that shut reflexively to block foreign objects, bright light, and drying winds, while spreading tear film with each blink.
- **Conjunctiva**: A transparent mucous membrane lining the inner eyelids and folding over the anterior sclera, producing lubricating mucus to prevent friction during eye movement.
- **Lacrimal Apparatus**: Consists of the lacrimal gland, which secretes tears containing water, salts, antibodies, and lysozyme to wash away pathogens, and a drainage system leading to the nasal cavity via the nasolacrimal duct.
- **Extrinsic Eye Muscles**: Six skeletal muscles (four rectus and two oblique) attached to the exterior of the eyeball, coordinating precise, conjugate movements in all visual fields.

headings.title: Tunics of the Eyeball: Fibrous and Vascular Layers
headings.content:
The wall of the eyeball is constructed from three distinct layers, or tunics. The outermost layer is the **fibrous tunic**, providing structural shape and physical protection. It is divided into the white, dense, irregular connective tissue **sclera** posteriorly, and the clear, avascular **cornea** anteriorly, which acts as the primary light-refracting surface of the eye.

Deep to the fibrous tunic lies the **vascular tunic** or **uvea**, composed of three regions:
1. **Choroid**: A highly vascular, pigmented middle layer that supplies nutrients to other ocular tissues and absorbs stray light to prevent visual blur.
2. **Ciliary Body**: A thickened ring of tissue containing smooth muscle that alters lens shape, and processes that secrete aqueous humor.
3. **Iris**: The colored, muscular diaphragm containing circular and radial smooth muscle fibers that regulate the aperture of the pupil, controlling light entry into the eye.

headings.title: The Retina and Neural Processing
headings.content:
The **retina** forms the innermost, delicate sensory tunic of the eye, transforming light energy into electrical nerve impulses. Structurally, it features an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural layer containing three main tiers of neurons: photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and ganglion cells.

- **Photoreceptors**: 
  - **Rods**: Highly sensitive to low light levels, specialized for grayscale night vision and peripheral detection.
  - **Cones**: Function best in bright light, mediating high-acuity color vision concentrated densely at the **fovea centralis**.

Axons of the ganglion cells converge at the **optic disc**—commonly called the blind spot because it lacks photoreceptors—to form the optic nerve exiting the globe. Local processing by horizontal and amacrine cells within the retinal layers refines contrast and sharpens visual signals before they travel onward to the brain.

headings.title: Internal Cavities, Humors, and Intraocular Pressure
headings.content:
The interior of the eye is divided into two distinct segments by the lens and ciliary body, maintaining structural rigidity and optical clarity through internal fluid dynamics.

| Segment | Cavity Fluid | Production and Drainage Site | Primary Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Anterior Segment | Aqueous Humor | Secreted by ciliary processes; drained via scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm) | Nourishes avascular lens and cornea; maintains intraocular pressure |
| Posterior Segment | Vitreous Humor | Formed during embryonic development; permanent gel | Supports posterior surface of lens; holds retina flat against choroid |

When the drainage of aqueous humor through the canal of Schlemm becomes blocked, fluid accumulates, elevating **intraocular pressure (IOP)**. Chronic elevation compresses retinal blood vessels and the optic nerve, a pathological condition known as **glaucoma** that can lead to irreversible blindness if untreated.

headings.title: Physiology of Vision: Refraction and Accommodation
headings.content:
Light rays traveling from an object must be bent, or **refracted**, so they converge precisely onto the retina to form a clear image. The cornea provides the fixed, major portion of refractive power, while the flexible lens allows for fine-tuning.

To view close objects clearly, the eye undergoes **accommodation**. The ciliary muscle contracts, releasing tension on the suspensory ligaments (zonules). This allows the elastic lens to bulge into a more convex shape, increasing its refractive power. Conversely, viewing distant objects relaxes the ciliary muscle, pulling the ligaments taut and flattening the lens.

Common refractive errors include **myopia** (nearsightedness), where the eyeball is too long and images focus in front of the retina, and **hyperopia** (farsightedness), where the eyeball is too short, focusing images behind the retina.

headings.title: Phototransduction and the Visual Pathway
headings.content:
Phototransduction is the conversion of light energy into electrical signals within the photoreceptor cells of the retina. The visual pigment in rods, called **rhodopsin**, consists of retinal (a light-absorbing molecule derived from vitamin A) bound to opsin protein. In the dark, rhodopsin is inactive, sodium channels remain open, and photoreceptors continuously release inhibitory neurotransmitters. When light strikes rhodopsin, retinal changes shape, triggering a biochemical cascade that closes sodium channels, hyperpolarizes the cell, and stops neurotransmitter release, thereby exciting the downstream bipolar cells.

From the retina, nerve impulses travel along the optic nerves to the **optic chiasm**, where fibers from the medial half of each retina cross over to the opposite side. The pathway continues via the optic tracts to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and finally to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe for conscious visual perception.
